cands.bio: Professor of political science at College of the Sequoias in Visalia and co-owner of his family's auto body shop. Visalia Unified school board trustee since December 2021. Born and raised in Bakersfield; Ph.D. from UC Santa Cruz. Won California's 22nd District in 2026, defeating incumbent David Valadao.

endorsements.text: Endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, Working Families Party, California Teachers Association, National Nurses United, Congressional Hispanic Caucus BOLD PAC, Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC, Latino Victory Fund, California Environmental Voters and Dolores Huerta.

cands.gaps: We found no record of Villegas's positions or actions on homestead property taxes, policing and law enforcement pay, gun laws, abortion, or vouchers and charter schools. We found no school board votes or other official actions on any of these topics. The only source for his data center moratorium is a Wikipedia summary with no date, and no primary statement was available. His teacher-pay record on the school board comes from his own survey answers, not from board records. We found no documented controversies about him personally and no foreign ties. The campaign website's issue pages were only partly readable, so some stated positions may be missing.

qual.background: Appointed to the Visalia Unified School District board in December 2021 and elected to a full term in November 2022. Political science professor at College of the Sequoias, co-owner of a family auto body shop, and earlier a journalist and community organizer.
qual.why: He has held local elected office and runs a small business, which fits the middle band. He has no legislative, executive or legal experience at the state or federal level.
qual.label: He has held local elected office and runs a small business, which fits the middle band. He has no legislative, executive or legal experience at the state or federal level.

clean-money.evidence: Said he has never taken corporate PAC money and pledged to ban corporate PACs and overturn Citizens United.

land-for-floridians.evidence: Said on his campaign website, "I will fight to end corporate ownership of single-family homes," and criticized Wall Street and corporate landlords buying up neighborhoods.

workers-first.evidence: Said current policies of blanket detention and deportation are unconstitutional, and called for a path to citizenship. Wikipedia adds that he supports a secure border and does not support abolishing ICE.

stop-data-centers.evidence: Wikipedia reports he supports a one-year moratorium on new data center construction and says data centers should pay the full cost of their own electricity.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: Said that as a school board trustee he fought for and won pay increases for teachers and school staff; this is his own account. He also said teachers deserve better salaries. No position on vouchers or charters was found.

slow-growth-protect-land.evidence: Said on his campaign website that national parks and wildlife conservation programs should be expanded and that selling off public lands should end.

prio.label: Matches 5 of 6 priorities; 0 backed by their record, 5 only promised

cands.bio: Dairy farmer and managing partner of Valadao Dairy in Hanford. Served in the California Assembly (District 30) 2010–2012. U.S. House member for California's 21st District 2013–2019, then again from 2021, now representing the 22nd District. Sat on the House Appropriations Committee.

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed by Ballotpedia include the Republican Party of California, IUOE Local 3 and Reform California.

cands.gaps: We found no documented stance from Valadao on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buyers, abortion, gun policy, police pay and pensions, or school vouchers and charters. We also found no specific bills or actions of his on growth and land protection, and no documented controversies or foreign ties in the pages we could read. The Ballotpedia page was cut off before its key-votes section. The campaign website text on his positions is mostly carried over from earlier campaigns. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey, so his own answers on many issues are missing.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.
